notes.text:
The reproach of Egypt — That is, uncircumcision, was both in truth, and in the opinion of the Jews, a matter of great reproach, and although this was a reproach common to most nations of the world, yet it is particularly called the reproach of Egypt, either,

1. because the other neighbouring nations, being the children of Abraham by the concubines, are supposed to have been circumcised, which the Egyptians at this time were not, as may be gathered from Exod. ii, 6, where they knew the child to be an Hebrew by this mark. Or

2. because they came out of Egypt, and were esteemed to be a sort of Egyptians, Num. xxii, 5, which they justly thought a great reproach; but by their circumcision they were now distinguished from them, and manifested to be another people. Or

3. because many of them lay under this reproach in Egypt, having wickedly neglected this duty there for worldly reasons; and others of them continued in the same shameful condition for many years in the wilderness. Gilgal - That is, rolling.

The passover — Which was their third passover: the first was in Egypt, Exod. xii, 11-24, the second at Mount Sinai, Num. ix, 1-5, the third here; for in their wilderness travels, these and all other sacrifices were neglected, Amos v, 25. While they were in the wilderness, they were denied the comfort of this ordinance, as a farther token of God's displeasure. But now God comforted them again, after the time that he had afflicted them.

Old corn — The corn of the last year, which the inhabitants of those parts had left in their barns, being fled into their strong cities, or other remoter parts. The morrow - That is, on the sixteenth day; for the passover was killed between the two evenings of the fourteenth day, and was eaten in that evening or night, which, according to the Jewish computation, whereby they begin their days at the evening, was a part of the fifteenth day, all which was the feast of the passover; and so the morrow of the sixteenth day, was the morrow after the passover, when they were obliged to offer unto God the first sheaf, and then were allowed to eat of the rest. Parched corn - Of that year's corn. which was most proper for that use. Self-same day - Having an eager desire to enjoy the fruits of the land. And this corn came very seasonably; for after the passover, they were to keep the feast of unleavened bread, which they could not do, when they had nothing but manna to live upon.

The manna ceased — Which God now withheld, to shew that Manna was not an ordinary production of nature, but an extraordinary and special gift of God to supply their necessity. And because God would not be prodigal of his favours, by working miracles where ordinary means were sufficient. The morrow - That is, on the seventeenth day.

glossa.text:
*And they ate,* etc. ((ADAM., hom. 6.)) But when the people went out of the land of Egypt, etc., *as far as* For how is it thought that, the better food ceasing, a worse succeeded.

((JUSTIN., Dialog. )) God in the beginning, before all creatures, begot out of himself a certain rational power, which is also called the Glory of the Lord, and sometimes the Son, Wisdom, Angel, Word, God, Lord. Sometimes also he calls himself the Master of the host, when he appeared in human form to Jesus the son of Nave.

*And he saw a man. ((ADAM., hom. 6 in Josue.))* It came to pass, when Jesus was in Jericho, etc., *as far as* who, having received a kingdom, returned.

notes.text: Imputeth — Whom God doth not charge with the guilt of his sins, but graciously pardons and accepts him in Christ. No guile - Who freely confesses all his sins, and turns from sin to God with all his heart.

Silence — From a full and open confession of my sins. Old - My spirit failed, and the strength of my body decayed. Roaring - Because of the continual horrors of my conscience, and sense of God's wrath.
Hand — Thy afflicting hand. My moisture - Was dried up.
The iniquity — The guilt of my sin.

For this — Upon the encouragement of my example. Found - In an acceptable and seasonable time, while God continues to offer grace and mercy. Waters - In the time of great calamities. Not come - So as to overwhelm him.
I will — This and the next verse seems to be the words of God, whom David brings in as returning this answer to his prayers. Mine eye - So Christ did St. Peter, when he turned and looked upon him.
Will not — Unless they be forced to it by a bit or bridle. And so all the ancient translators understand it.

Sorrows — This is an argument to enforce the foregoing admonition. The Psalmist exhorts the righteous to praise God, for his truth, justice and goodness, ver. 1-5, For creating the world, ver. 6-9. For his providence in governing it, ver. 10-17. For his peculiar favour to his people, encouraging them to trust in him, ver. 18-22.

glossa.text: *Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven,* etc. ((AUG.)) Not those in whom he finds no sin, but those to whom he forgives it. *Iniquities.* He means the tinder of sin, namely concupiscence, etc., *as far as* but that sin may be no more. ((HIERON.)) Iniquities, before faith and baptism: sin, after faith and baptism.

*Blessed is the man.* ((HIERON.)) To whom God forgives, for not of himself. He covers it, that it be not revealed in the judgment; and so it will not be imputed unto punishment. There is no guile in him that accuses himself: he holds in the heart what he confesses here with the mouth.

*Blessed:* because formerly, not confessing to God, I came into sin, while I cried out, if I did any good.

*I was silent.* ((AUG.)) He who will not confess his sins labours without cause in the defence of sins: and since in this he also boasts of his merits, his strength fails the more. ((CASS.)) *Blessed is he to whom he hath not imputed.* To some, who have grievous sins, God imputes them; to others he does not impute them, through mercy, even though they have some — namely to those who do not proclaim themselves just when they are evil, but acknowledging themselves make satisfaction. This I now profess, but formerly: *Because I was silent,* etc. ((AUG.)) Or, *I was silent,* as to sin with my voice, *while I cried out all the day:* while the penalty of sin, or an inward blinding, showed me a sinner, or while my evil life cried out, though I was silent, whether I had done any good.

*While I cried out all the day,* etc. Although a man be not conscious to himself of anything, yet he is not just: for who understands his offences? Whence: *There is a just man that perisheth in his own justice.* And the Apostle: *I am conscious to myself of nothing,* etc.
*The thorn is fastened in.* ((CASS.)) *The thorn,* which lifts up the whole body, that is, pride. ((AUG.)) Likewise *misery,* etc., *as far as: in the hands of a drunken man.*
*My sin.* Diapsalma. Confession, whence pardon, as above the growing old from governance. *I have made known.* ((CASS.)) For *I said* before, etc., *as far as* and God hears.

*For this shall he pray.* ((ID.)) Diapsalma. Commending repentance, he says it is common to all the saints; which sundry sects reject, against whom he flees for refuge to God. ((AUG.)) *For this.* Therefore every saint prays, because thou hast forgiven, otherwise he would not be a saint. *In the time,* etc. It is the time of grace, the law, pressing and convicting the guilty, compelled them to cry out, grace heals. *But yet in the flood,* etc. ((AUG.)) Although the saint pray, etc., *as far as* the saint will pray, saying: *Thou art a refuge. To him.* That is, to God, for he changes the person, as often. They do not draw near who say that fate makes them sin, or fortune, which rules all things, or the people of darkness, which rebels against God.

*I will give thee understanding.* ((ID.)) Diapsalma. It is answered to the penitent: *I will give thee understanding,* etc. Behold a psalm of understanding, lest the suppliant be thought neglected, with God for witness. *Thou, deliver.* ((CASS.)) Thou who hast promised, *I will give thee understanding.* Or Christ answers the penitent: A glad end, God gives understanding: whence he exhorts others to the same.

*Become ye not as the horse and the mule,* etc. ((AUG.)) Having received understanding, this penitent turns himself to the proud who defend their sins: therefore you, whom I invite, etc. *The horse,* the untamed Gentile; *the mule,* the Jew slow to believe. ((CASS.)) *The horse,* without discernment of its riders; *the mule,* takes any burdens whatever, etc., *as far as* that is, boasting of one's own strength. *Their jaws.* Or, *the jaws* with which they chew, that is, give victuals more sparingly, that being compelled by necessity they may return. ((AUG.)) Or, thou wilt break them here, and in the world to come there will be many scourges. Or: *Become ye not as the horse,* because there are many scourges here and in the world to come. *Who come not near to thee.* ((CASS.)) For there are those who, if they sin through the weakness of the flesh, do not withdraw from devout prayers.

*Many are the scourges of the sinner,* etc. ((AUG.)) After the bridle, scourges are added for taming, lest he be of those unpunished ones to whom a roving licence of their own way is now given: so this man above said that he was tamed.

notes.text: So that we from this time — That we knew the love of Christ. Know no one - Neither ourselves, nor you, neither the rest of the apostles, Gal. ii, 6, nor any other person. After the flesh - According to his former state, country, descent, nobility, riches, power, wisdom. We fear not the great. We regard not the rich or wise. We account not the least less than ourselves. We consider all, only in order to save all. Who is he that thus knows no one after the flesh? ln what land do these Christians live? Yea, if we have known even Christ after the flesh - So as to love him barely with a natural love, so as to glory in having conversed with him on earth, so as to expect only temporal benefits from him.

Therefore if any one be in Christ — A true believer in him. There is a new creation - Only the power that makes a world can make a Christian. And when he is so created, the old things are passed away - Of their own accord, even as snow in spring. Behold - The present, visible, undeniable change! All things are become new - He has new life, new senses, new faculties, new affections, new appetites, new ideas and conceptions. His whole tenor of action and conversation is new, and he lives, as it were, in a new world. God, men, the whole creation, heaven, earth, and all therein, appear in a new light, and stand related to him in a new manner, since he was created anew in Christ Jesus.
And all these new things are from God, considered under this very notion, as reconciling us — The world, 2 Cor. v, 19, to himself.

Namely — The sum of which is, God - The whole Godhead, but more eminently God the Father. Was in Christ, reconciling the world - Which was before at enmity with God. To himself - So taking away that enmity, which could no otherwise be removed than by the blood of the Son of God.

Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ-we beseech you in Christ's stead — Herein the apostle might appear to some "transported beyond himself." In general he uses a more calm, sedate kind of exhortation, as in the beginning of the next chapter. What unparalleled condescension and divinely tender mercies are displayed in this verse! Did the judge ever beseech a condemned criminal to accept of pardon? Does the creditor ever beseech a ruined debtor to receive an acquittance in full? Yet our almighty Lord, and our eternal Judge, not only vouchsafes to offer these blessings, but invites us, entreats us, and, with the most tender importunity, solicits us, not to reject them.

He made him a sin offering, who knew no sin — A commendation peculiar to Christ. For us - Who knew no righteousness, who were inwardly and outwardly nothing but sin; who must have been consumed by the divine justice, had not this atonement been made for our sins. That we might be made the righteousness of God through him - Might through him be invested with that righteousness, first imputed to us, then implanted in us, which is in every sense the righteousness of God.

glossa.text: *We know no man.* That is, we praise. *According to the flesh.* That is, one seeking his own things, not those which are Christ's: temporal things, not eternal. Nor ought anyone to do this, because although Christ was mortal as I am, whereby I thought him to be a man only, while I was unbelieving: yet now he is immortal, and so we are secure of the reward. If therefore anyone is born again new in Christ, for him mortality has already passed away in hope, and shall pass away, and a new immortality shall be given. Or, if anyone is new, the old law has passed away for him, and he has a new one. *No man not according to the flesh.* He holds the life to come with a hope so sure, as though it were already present: which was fulfilled in Christ rising again, which is not according to the flesh: not but that we shall rise again in the same substance of flesh, but that it will not be in the same quality of corruption, which is signified by the name of flesh. *And if we have known according to the flesh.* Because although, while he was unbelieving, he understood Christ to have been promised in the law according to the flesh, so that he observed the things of the law and commanded them to be kept: yet nevertheless after his conversion he does not now believe it to be so any longer, but the shadow wholly ceases.

*The old things.* Wholly the Old Testament and all things pertaining to the old man, as such. *New things.* There have come the New Testament, and all things of the new man. *The old things.* As the error of idolatry, upon which the knowledge of the one true God has followed.

*God was in Christ.* By this it is understood that the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father, because their substance is one. There is unity, where there is no diversity: and therefore the one is in the other, because both their image and their likeness is one.
*Be ye reconciled.* We are reconciled by confessing our sins, and by repenting to him who reconciles us to himself.

notes.text: All the publicans — That is, all who were in that place. It seems our Lord was in some town of Galilee of the Gentiles, from whence he afterward went to Jerusalem, chap. xvii, 11.

He spake — Three parables of the same import: for the sheep, the piece of silver, and the lost son, all declare (in direct contrariety to the Pharisees and scribes) in what manner God receiveth sinners.

hymns.title: Deck thyself, my soul, with gladness
Be present at our table, Lord
Come to the table of mercy
Gentile or Jew, servant or free
As we gather at your table
Come, let us eat, for now the feast is spread

registers.label: Spare
lines: While we were still far off, God saw us and ran.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
We squandered the inheritance and came home in rags.
The Father has put a robe around our shoulders.
The calf is killed; the feast is ready.
We were lost, and we are found. Come, let us worship.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: See the father on the road, robe hiked up, running — running while the son is still a long way off.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
You who came home rehearsing your apology, you who fed the pigs and dreamed of bread — the arms are already around you.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
The best robe, the ring, the sandals, the fatted calf — for this child was dead and is alive again.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So come in from the field, elder and younger alike; the music has started and the table is full.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: While we were far off, the Father ran and threw his arms around us.
Turn us, O God, and we will return.
He puts the best robe on our shoulders and a ring on our hand.
Turn us, O God, and we will return.
We were dead and are alive; come to the feast.
Turn us, O God, and we will return. Amen.
